vignette:
Frank, a 63-year-old physician, had always defined himself by his composure and clinical detachment. That was before the attack. He was on the number 12 bus, heading home after a long shift, when the vehicle ahead of it was consumed by a fireball. The blast shattered the bus windows, and the next moments were a chaotic blur of smoke, screaming, and the smell of burning fuel. He remembers trying to help, his medical instincts kicking in, but being shoved back by police officers whose shouted commands felt as violent as the explosion itself. He was just one person in a terrified crowd, being herded away from the carnage like an animal.

In the months that followed, the world began to reconfigure itself in Frank’s mind. The change was insidious. He started driving to the hospital, telling his wife it was more convenient, but the truth was that the thought of setting foot on a bus filled him with a cold dread. This avoidance was a symptom of a deeper conviction taking root: that the world was not a place of manageable risks, but one of imminent, predatory danger. He had come to believe that people were fundamentally unknowable and could not be trusted; the attacker, he reasoned, must have looked like any other person on the street just moments before destroying so many lives.

This pervasive sense of a dangerous world means Frank can never truly be at ease. At home, the place he once considered his sanctuary, he finds himself perpetually on guard, listening intently for any sound that might signal an intruder. The creak of a floorboard or the rustle of leaves outside the window is enough to put him on high alert. This constant state of threat monitoring feeds his irritability, which simmers just below the surface and erupts in sharp, angry outbursts that often seem to come from nowhere, startling his wife and himself. He sees these outbursts not as a symptom, but as a necessary defense in a world that requires constant vigilance.

The cycle is self-sustaining and has tightened its grip over the past year. A news report on television showing any kind of violence (a trigger) is no longer just a sad story; for Frank, it serves as immediate, visceral proof that his life has been permanently destroyed and that safety is an illusion (Negative Appraisals). This deeply held belief that he is unsafe then fuels his hypervigilance (Threat). Conversely, the exhaustion from a sleepless night spent monitoring sounds in the house (Threat) only reinforces his despairing conclusion that his life is ruined beyond repair (Negative Appraisals). This appraisal, this certainty that the world is hostile, also makes him exquisitely sensitive to perceived challenges to his autonomy. When a hospital administrator gives him a direct instruction (a trigger), he doesn't hear a routine request; he hears the echo of the police officer’s barked orders on the day of the bombing, a command that strips him of control and reinforces his belief that others are not to be trusted (Negative Appraisals).

His world has become small and suffocating. His colleagues at the hospital have grown wary of his temper, and his wife confesses she feels like she is walking on eggshells. The decision to seek therapy was precipitated by an incident at work where he shouted at a junior resident for asking a simple question, an overreaction so disproportionate it left him shaken and ashamed. Frank arrived at his first session not with a specific goal, but with a profound sense of loss. He is terrified that the calm, competent man he once was is gone forever, replaced by this angry, frightened stranger. His deepest hope is simply to feel safe in his own home again, to silence the alarms that ring incessantly in his head.
